answer.text: The historical development of long short-term memory networks begins with a formal diagnosis of a training failure.

Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis first identified the vanishing gradient problem, showing that as errors propagate backward through many layers or time steps, the numerical signal shrinks exponentially and early layers stop learning.
Yoshua Bengio and colleagues formalized this in 1994, proving that learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is fundamentally difficult for standard recurrent networks.

Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber's 1997 paper "Long Short-Term Memory" solved this by introducing gated memory cells with input and output gates that let error signals flow unchanged across time steps.
Felix Gers extended the architecture in 2000 by adding a forget gate, producing the LSTM variant that became the field standard.

Schmidhuber's group at IDSIA, working with students including Gers, Fred Cummins, and Alex Graves, then pushed LSTM into practice, and a Connectionist Temporal Classification-trained LSTM won multiple 2009 handwriting-recognition competitions, the first RNN to do so.

This lineage carried directly into commercial speech recognition: Google's voice search adopted LSTM-CTC acoustic models for real-time streaming transcription, and Microsoft's 2016 conversational speech system, also LSTM-based, reached a historic 5.9 percent error rate matching human transcribers.
By 2022 Schmidhuber noted LSTM running in billions of smartphones and powering Facebook's translation of roughly 30 billion messages per week, illustrating how far the 1997 mechanism traveled.

The encoder-decoder architecture emerged independently but on the same foundation in 2014, when Ilya Sutskever's team and Kyunghyun Cho's team each proposed pairing two LSTM-based recurrent networks, one encoding a source sequence into a fixed-length vector and one decoding it into a target sequence, for English-French translation.

Cho's group also showed that this fixed-length "context vector" degraded badly on long sentences, a limitation Dzmitry Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio addressed in 2015 with an attention mechanism that lets the decoder softly search all encoder hidden states rather than compressing everything into one vector.

Attention was quickly generalized beyond translation, notably by Xu and colleagues for image captioning in 2015, and Google deployed the attention-augmented encoder-decoder in production Translate by 2016.

The architecture's final milestone arrived in 2017, when the Transformer paper discarded recurrence entirely, replacing the RNN encoder-decoder with parallelizable self-attention while keeping the encoder-decoder attention structure, improving English-German translation by over two BLEU points.

These technical advances made three applications practical at scale: Google's Neural Machine Translation system cut translation errors 55 to 85 percent and serves roughly 18 million Chinese-English translations daily using TensorFlow and TPUs.
Google Translate now supports over 100 languages, aiding cross-border communication and helping preserve endangered languages through crowd-sourced community translation.
SwiftKey's neural predictive keyboard, deployed on over 300 million devices, demonstrated how sequence models made everyday typing faster.

Accessibility applications multiplied: Voiceitt and Google's Parrotron normalize impaired speech, GnoSys translates sign language, DeepMind's lip-reading system was trained on 5,000 hours of television, and Microsoft's Seeing AI narrates surroundings for visually impaired users, while Ava, RogerVoice, and Google's Project Euphonia extend transcription and speech-impairment support under accessibility law.

Globalization and accessibility gains carry an employment cost: professional translators increasingly work as Post-Editors correcting machine output, Google's own French-English BLEU scores approach human parity, 41 percent of surveyed workers fear job loss to automation, and DARPA's Bolt project shows the same seq2seq technology repurposed for military language operations, a reminder of dual-use risk.

Broader economic analysis argues these are not law-of-nature outcomes but choices; the MIT Inclusive Innovation Challenge exemplifies policy responses aimed at spreading productivity gains rather than concentrating them.
Ethical scrutiny centers on three recurring problems.

Training-data bias is well documented in NLP scholarship covering word embeddings, coreference resolution, and machine translation, and it produced a concrete failure when Amazon's AI recruiting tool penalized wording associated with certain candidates and was ultimately scrapped.

Unequal access compounds this: because most training data and NLP research originates in English-speaking, well-funded institutions, "decolonising AI" advocates note resulting bias, and grassroots projects like FFR and Masakhane build machine translation for African languages, while a literacy gap left Yemeni communities unable to access aid tied to biometric systems.

Misuse risks include GPT-style language generation exploited for disinformation and deepfakes, and government AI surveillance exemplified by China's social credit system, both compounded by engagement-driven algorithms that create disinformation-amplifying echo chambers.
Formal ethical frameworks respond directly to these harms.

IEEE's "Ethically Aligned Design" compiled over 80 recommendations across eight sections covering personal data management, autonomous weapons, and economic ramifications, produced by more than 100 contributors and refined into a second version by 2017.
The 2017 Asilomar AI Principles complement this with 23 principles emphasizing transparency, accountability, and shared benefit, alongside the industry-led Partnership on AI.

Comparing the two architectures historically, LSTM is the older, general-purpose sequence-memory mechanism from 1997, while the encoder-decoder framework is a 2014 application-level architecture that initially depended on LSTM cells as its internal engine before attention and Transformers replaced recurrence altogether.

Technically, LSTM solves within-sequence memory via gating, whereas encoder-decoder solves sequence-to-sequence mapping via a learned intermediate representation, meaning the two innovations are complementary layers of the same translation and transcription pipelines rather than competitors.

Societally, LSTM's impact is diffuse and infrastructural, embedded in billions of devices for everyday recognition, while encoder-decoder's impact is more visible and institutional, reshaping translation industries, disinformation ecosystems, and platform-scale communication.

Synthesizing the ten case studies, GNMT, Google Translate's globalization role, Microsoft's speech-recognition parity, SwiftKey's predictive text, the Amazon hiring-bias failure, GPT-3 disinformation risk, China's AI surveillance, the assistive-technology ecosystem, translator displacement, and the African-language digital-divide projects, together shows that architectural breakthroughs diffuse unevenly and inherit the biases and access gaps of their training data and funding sources.

Responsible innovation therefore requires pairing technical safeguards with governance: IEEE- and Asilomar-style principles for transparency and accountability, deliberate low-resource-language investment to close the digital divide, post-editor and reskilling pathways for displaced workers, and detection research for deepfakes and disinformation.
Ethical innovation strategy is thus less about restraining LSTM or encoder-decoder capability and more about redistributing who designs, trains, and benefits from it.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

The historical development of long short-term memory networks begins with a formal diagnosis of a training failure.

Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis first identified the vanishing gradient problem, showing that as errors propagate backward through many layers or time steps, the numerical signal shrinks exponentially and early layers stop learning.
[shard_03952_21424]

Yoshua Bengio and colleagues formalized this in 1994, proving that learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is fundamentally difficult for standard recurrent networks.
[shard_03952_21424]

Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber's 1997 paper "Long Short-Term Memory" solved this by introducing gated memory cells with input and output gates that let error signals flow unchanged across time steps.
[shard_02149_69316] [shard_04044_33411]

Felix Gers extended the architecture in 2000 by adding a forget gate, producing the LSTM variant that became the field standard.
[shard_04044_33411] [shard_02149_69316]

Schmidhuber's group at IDSIA, working with students including Gers, Fred Cummins, and Alex Graves, then pushed LSTM into practice, and a Connectionist Temporal Classification-trained LSTM won multiple 2009 handwriting-recognition competitions, the first RNN to do so.
[shard_02149_69316]

This lineage carried directly into commercial speech recognition: Google's voice search adopted LSTM-CTC acoustic models for real-time streaming transcription, and Microsoft's 2016 conversational speech system, also LSTM-based, reached a historic 5.9 percent error rate matching human transcribers.
[shard_06073_43903] [shard_04184_78963]

By 2022 Schmidhuber noted LSTM running in billions of smartphones and powering Facebook's translation of roughly 30 billion messages per week, illustrating how far the 1997 mechanism traveled.
[shard_04237_34887]

The encoder-decoder architecture emerged independently but on the same foundation in 2014, when Ilya Sutskever's team and Kyunghyun Cho's team each proposed pairing two LSTM-based recurrent networks, one encoding a source sequence into a fixed-length vector and one decoding it into a target sequence, for English-French translation.
[shard_01205_10962]

Cho's group also showed that this fixed-length "context vector" degraded badly on long sentences, a limitation Dzmitry Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio addressed in 2015 with an attention mechanism that lets the decoder softly search all encoder hidden states rather than compressing everything into one vector.
[shard_02007_31880] [shard_01205_10962]

Attention was quickly generalized beyond translation, notably by Xu and colleagues for image captioning in 2015, and Google deployed the attention-augmented encoder-decoder in production Translate by 2016.
[shard_01205_10962] [shard_04582_54688]

The architecture's final milestone arrived in 2017, when the Transformer paper discarded recurrence entirely, replacing the RNN encoder-decoder with parallelizable self-attention while keeping the encoder-decoder attention structure, improving English-German translation by over two BLEU points.
[shard_04582_54688]

These technical advances made three applications practical at scale: Google's Neural Machine Translation system cut translation errors 55 to 85 percent and serves roughly 18 million Chinese-English translations daily using TensorFlow and TPUs.
[shard_04398_57722]

Google Translate now supports over 100 languages, aiding cross-border communication and helping preserve endangered languages through crowd-sourced community translation.
[shard_00710_415]

SwiftKey's neural predictive keyboard, deployed on over 300 million devices, demonstrated how sequence models made everyday typing faster.
[shard_04197_61456]

Accessibility applications multiplied: Voiceitt and Google's Parrotron normalize impaired speech, GnoSys translates sign language, DeepMind's lip-reading system was trained on 5,000 hours of television, and Microsoft's Seeing AI narrates surroundings for visually impaired users, while Ava, RogerVoice, and Google's Project Euphonia extend transcription and speech-impairment support under accessibility law.
[shard_02969_3272] [shard_03940_47499]

Globalization and accessibility gains carry an employment cost: professional translators increasingly work as Post-Editors correcting machine output, Google's own French-English BLEU scores approach human parity, 41 percent of surveyed workers fear job loss to automation, and DARPA's Bolt project shows the same seq2seq technology repurposed for military language operations, a reminder of dual-use risk.
[shard_01490_12018] [shard_06158_56384]

Broader economic analysis argues these are not law-of-nature outcomes but choices; the MIT Inclusive Innovation Challenge exemplifies policy responses aimed at spreading productivity gains rather than concentrating them.
[shard_03870_53586]

Training-data bias is well documented in NLP scholarship covering word embeddings, coreference resolution, and machine translation, and it produced a concrete failure when Amazon's AI recruiting tool penalized wording associated with certain candidates and was ultimately scrapped.
[shard_00322_54999] [shard_04244_58814]

Unequal access compounds this: because most training data and NLP research originates in English-speaking, well-funded institutions, "decolonising AI" advocates note resulting bias, and grassroots projects like FFR and Masakhane build machine translation for African languages, while a literacy gap left Yemeni communities unable to access aid tied to biometric systems.
[shard_05566_30468] [shard_04171_12427]

[shard_00763_61811] [shard_03505_84175]

[shard_04390_49984] [shard_03549_31569]

[shard_03549_31569]

Synthesizing the ten case studies, GNMT, Google Translate's globalization role, Microsoft's speech-recognition parity, SwiftKey's predictive text, the Amazon hiring-bias failure, GPT-3 disinformation risk, China's AI surveillance, the assistive-technology ecosystem, translator displacement, and the African-language digital-divide projects, together shows that architectural breakthroughs diffuse unevenly and inherit the biases and access gaps of their training data and funding sources.
[shard_04398_57722] [shard_04244_58814] [shard_05566_30468]

Responsible innovation therefore requires pairing technical safeguards with governance: IEEE- and Asilomar-style principles for transparency and accountability, deliberate low-resource-language investment to close the digital divide, post-editor and reskilling pathways for displaced workers, and detection research for deepfakes and disinformation.
[shard_04390_49984] [shard_03549_31569] [shard_00763_61811]

Ethical innovation strategy is thus less about restraining LSTM or encoder-decoder capability and more about redistributing who designs, trains, and benefits from it.

answer.text: The historical development of long short-term memory networks begins with a formal diagnosis of a training failure.

Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis first identified the vanishing gradient problem, showing that as errors propagate backward through many layers or time steps, the numerical signal shrinks exponentially and early layers stop learning.
Yoshua Bengio and colleagues formalized this in 1994, proving that learning long-term dependencies with gradient descent is fundamentally difficult for standard recurrent networks.

Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber's 1997 paper "Long Short-Term Memory" solved this by introducing gated memory cells with input and output gates that let error signals flow unchanged across time steps.
Felix Gers extended the architecture in 2000 by adding a forget gate, producing the LSTM variant that became the field standard.

Schmidhuber's group at IDSIA, working with students including Gers, Fred Cummins, and Alex Graves, then pushed LSTM into practice, and a Connectionist Temporal Classification-trained LSTM won multiple 2009 handwriting-recognition competitions, the first RNN to do so.

This lineage carried directly into commercial speech recognition: Google's voice search adopted LSTM-CTC acoustic models for real-time streaming transcription, and Microsoft's 2016 conversational speech system, also LSTM-based, reached a historic 5.9 percent error rate matching human transcribers.
By 2022 Schmidhuber noted LSTM running in billions of smartphones and powering Facebook's translation of roughly 30 billion messages per week, illustrating how far the 1997 mechanism traveled.

The encoder-decoder architecture emerged independently but on the same foundation in 2014, when Ilya Sutskever's team and Kyunghyun Cho's team each proposed pairing two LSTM-based recurrent networks, one encoding a source sequence into a fixed-length vector and one decoding it into a target sequence, for English-French translation.

Cho's group also showed that this fixed-length "context vector" degraded badly on long sentences, a limitation Dzmitry Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio addressed in 2015 with an attention mechanism that lets the decoder softly search all encoder hidden states rather than compressing everything into one vector.

Attention was quickly generalized beyond translation, notably by Xu and colleagues for image captioning in 2015, and Google deployed the attention-augmented encoder-decoder in production Translate by 2016.

The architecture's final milestone arrived in 2017, when the Transformer paper discarded recurrence entirely, replacing the RNN encoder-decoder with parallelizable self-attention while keeping the encoder-decoder attention structure, improving English-German translation by over two BLEU points.

These technical advances made three applications practical at scale: Google's Neural Machine Translation system cut translation errors 55 to 85 percent and serves roughly 18 million Chinese-English translations daily using TensorFlow and TPUs.
Google Translate now supports over 100 languages, aiding cross-border communication and helping preserve endangered languages through crowd-sourced community translation.
SwiftKey's neural predictive keyboard, deployed on over 300 million devices, demonstrated how sequence models made everyday typing faster.

Accessibility applications multiplied: Voiceitt and Google's Parrotron normalize impaired speech, GnoSys translates sign language, DeepMind's lip-reading system was trained on 5,000 hours of television, and Microsoft's Seeing AI narrates surroundings for visually impaired users, while Ava, RogerVoice, and Google's Project Euphonia extend transcription and speech-impairment support under accessibility law.

Globalization and accessibility gains carry an employment cost: professional translators increasingly work as Post-Editors correcting machine output, Google's own French-English BLEU scores approach human parity, 41 percent of surveyed workers fear job loss to automation, and DARPA's Bolt project shows the same seq2seq technology repurposed for military language operations, a reminder of dual-use risk.

Broader economic analysis argues these are not law-of-nature outcomes but choices; the MIT Inclusive Innovation Challenge exemplifies policy responses aimed at spreading productivity gains rather than concentrating them.
Ethical scrutiny centers on three recurring problems.

Training-data bias is well documented in NLP scholarship covering word embeddings, coreference resolution, and machine translation, and it produced a concrete failure when Amazon's AI recruiting tool penalized wording associated with certain candidates and was ultimately scrapped.

Unequal access compounds this: because most training data and NLP research originates in English-speaking, well-funded institutions, "decolonising AI" advocates note resulting bias, and grassroots projects like FFR and Masakhane build machine translation for African languages, while a literacy gap left Yemeni communities unable to access aid tied to biometric systems.

Misuse risks include GPT-style language generation exploited for disinformation and deepfakes, and government AI surveillance exemplified by China's social credit system, both compounded by engagement-driven algorithms that create disinformation-amplifying echo chambers.
Formal ethical frameworks respond directly to these harms.

IEEE's "Ethically Aligned Design" compiled over 80 recommendations across eight sections covering personal data management, autonomous weapons, and economic ramifications, produced by more than 100 contributors and refined into a second version by 2017.
The 2017 Asilomar AI Principles complement this with 23 principles emphasizing transparency, accountability, and shared benefit, alongside the industry-led Partnership on AI.

Comparing the two architectures historically, LSTM is the older, general-purpose sequence-memory mechanism from 1997, while the encoder-decoder framework is a 2014 application-level architecture that initially depended on LSTM cells as its internal engine before attention and Transformers replaced recurrence altogether.

Technically, LSTM solves within-sequence memory via gating, whereas encoder-decoder solves sequence-to-sequence mapping via a learned intermediate representation, meaning the two innovations are complementary layers of the same translation and transcription pipelines rather than competitors.

Societally, LSTM's impact is diffuse and infrastructural, embedded in billions of devices for everyday recognition, while encoder-decoder's impact is more visible and institutional, reshaping translation industries, disinformation ecosystems, and platform-scale communication.

Synthesizing the ten case studies, GNMT, Google Translate's globalization role, Microsoft's speech-recognition parity, SwiftKey's predictive text, the Amazon hiring-bias failure, GPT-3 disinformation risk, China's AI surveillance, the assistive-technology ecosystem, translator displacement, and the African-language digital-divide projects, together shows that architectural breakthroughs diffuse unevenly and inherit the biases and access gaps of their training data and funding sources.

Responsible innovation therefore requires pairing technical safeguards with governance: IEEE- and Asilomar-style principles for transparency and accountability, deliberate low-resource-language investment to close the digital divide, post-editor and reskilling pathways for displaced workers, and detection research for deepfakes and disinformation.
Ethical innovation strategy is thus less about restraining LSTM or encoder-decoder capability and more about redistributing who designs, trains, and benefits from it.
